info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 12.2: Deterministic Intertextual Discovery and Linked Web Annotation.

name.text: 01 Question: The Computational Turn in Intertextual Scholarship

questiontext.text: How do deterministic text-reuse algorithms overcome the historical limitations of manual intertextual commentary?

generalfeedback.text: Deterministic algorithms eliminate human memory bottlenecks and canonical bias by scanning massive historical corpora systematically for textual reuse.

answer.text: They eliminate human memory bottlenecks and canonical bias by scanning massive historical corpora systematically for shared linguistic tokens.

feedback.text: Correct. Algorithms evaluate entire multi-million-word corpora without human cognitive fatigue or selective memory, surfacing allusions in obscure as well as canonical authors.

answer.text: They automatically write interpretive commentary essays without requiring human domain expertise.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Deterministic algorithms discover candidate text reuse; human scholars must interpret and evaluate the literary connection.

answer.text: They restrict searches exclusively to famous canonical authors like Homer and Vergil.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Manual scholarship suffered from canonical bias; algorithms treat all texts in a corpus uniformly.

answer.text: They convert ancient poetic meter into modern rhyming English verse.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Text-reuse algorithms scan and align linguistic tokens, not produce poetic translations.

name.text: 02 Question: The Mechanics of Text Reuse: Lexical, Syntactic, and Thematic

questiontext.text: Why must deterministic algorithms abstract inflected surface words into standardized dictionary lemmas?

generalfeedback.text: Deterministic intertextual discovery requires abstracting inflected surface words into standardized lemmas to detect shared vocabulary across grammatical variations.

answer.text: In inflected languages like Greek and Latin, grammatical variation alters surface word forms while the core lexical borrowing remains identical.

feedback.text: Correct. Authors frequently allude to model texts using different grammatical cases, tenses, or moods, which exact string matching fails to detect.

answer.text: Lemmatization translates ancient Greek words into Latin equivalents to enable cross-language comparisons.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Lemmatization maps inflected word forms to their dictionary headword within the same language.

answer.text: Lemmatization deletes vowels to compress text files for high-speed transmission across networks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Lemmatization groups morphological forms together, not compresses text by removing vowels.

answer.text: Standard XML parsers refuse to parse inflected words unless they are converted to nominative singulars.

feedback.text: Incorrect. XML parsers are indifferent to grammar; lemmatization is a linguistic retrieval step.

name.text: 03 Question: The Tesserae Project: Architecture and Principles

questiontext.text: What foundational philological principle governs the discovery engine of the Tesserae Project?

generalfeedback.text: Tesserae discovers classical allusions by identifying pairs of texts that share rare lemmas clustered in close syntactic proximity.

answer.text: Rare words placed in close syntactic proximity carry a vastly higher probability of intentional literary allusion than common words spread far apart.

feedback.text: Correct. Tesserae's scoring formula pairs inverted corpus frequency (rarity) with syntactic distance (phrase density) to separate genuine allusions from noise.

answer.text: Every shared word between two texts, regardless of frequency or distance, represents an intentional quotation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Common words like prepositions or conjunctions co-occur constantly by statistical chance without signifying an allusion.

answer.text: Allusions can only occur if an ancient author explicitly names the source poet in a prefatory formula.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Ancient authors routinely engaged in unacknowledged imitation (mimesis) and subtle allusion without naming sources.

answer.text: Texts sharing identical rhyming schemes are automatically classified as direct literary copies.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Classical Greek and Latin verse relied on quantitative meter rather than modern end-rhyme.

name.text: 04 Question: Preprocessing for Intertextual Matching

questiontext.text: Why does the Tesserae preprocessing pipeline include enclitic resolution (e.g., detaching -que in Latin)?

generalfeedback.text: Textual preprocessing strips punctuation, separates enclitics, and resolves inflected words to lemmas to prepare corpora for algorithmic cross-comparison.

answer.text: Attached enclitics alter the surface word form, causing an inflected token like virumque to fail matching a parallel occurrence of virum.

feedback.text: Correct. Splitting enclitics into independent tokens ensures that root words and enclitic conjunctions are indexed and matched accurately.

answer.text: Enclitics contain secret cryptographic signatures that prevent text matching algorithms from executing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Enclitics are standard grammatical particles, not cryptographic signatures.

answer.text: Modern database engines cannot store words containing hyphenated suffixes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Enclitics attach directly without hyphens; splitting them resolves morphological token boundaries.

answer.text: Enclitics indicate that a manuscript line was copied by an unauthorized apprentice scribe.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Enclitics are standard grammatical features of classical Greek and Latin morphology.

name.text: 05 Question: The Tesserae Scoring Metric: Frequency and Density

questiontext.text: In the Tesserae scoring formula, what mathematical roles do the numerator and denominator play?

generalfeedback.text: The Tesserae scoring metric assigns high numerical values to rare shared words clustered closely together, elevating significant allusions above background noise.

answer.text: The numerator sums the inverted corpus frequencies of shared lemmas (rewarding rarity), while the denominator sums token distances (penalizing spread).

feedback.text: Correct. High scores result when shared words are extremely rare (large 1/f in numerator) and tightly clustered in both texts (small d in denominator).

answer.text: The numerator counts total manuscript pages, and the denominator calculates the author's year of birth.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The metric is based purely on linguistic corpus frequency and syntactic token distance.

answer.text: The numerator calculates alphabetical letter count, and the denominator counts the number of commas in the verse.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The score evaluates lexical rarity and phrase density, not raw character counts or punctuation.

answer.text: The numerator multiplies the price of the edition, and the denominator calculates the number of footnotes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The Tesserae scoring metric is a quantitative measure of linguistic and spatial similarity.

name.text: 06 Question: Calculating Rarity: TF-IDF and Inverted Corpus Frequency

questiontext.text: How does inverted corpus frequency ($1/f$) computationally mirror human philological intuition?

generalfeedback.text: Inverted frequency weighting computationally mirrors human philological intuition by suppressing high-frequency function words and elevating distinctive lexical signatures.

answer.text: It dynamically suppresses high-frequency grammatical function words while elevating distinctive, rare lexical signatures.

feedback.text: Correct. Philologists instinctively ignore common words like 'and' or 'in' to focus on distinctive, rare vocabulary; 1/f weights words inversely to their frequency.

answer.text: It automatically highlights grammatical errors in yellow and green in the web browser.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Inverted frequency is an information retrieval weighting calculation, not a visual error-highlighting tool.

answer.text: It ensures that every word in a historical language occurs exactly the same number of times.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Natural language follows Zipf's Law; 1/f accounts for this unequal distribution.

answer.text: It deletes low-frequency words from the database to save server disk space.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Low-frequency words are the most valuable evidence for literary allusions and receive the highest weights.

name.text: 07 Question: Calculating Phrase Density: Distance-Based Decay Functions

questiontext.text: Why does the Tesserae algorithm incorporate a distance divisor ($d_T + d_S$) in its denominator?

generalfeedback.text: Distance-based scoring penalizes diffuse word co-occurrences and rewards tight phrase density, capturing the compact acoustic nature of literary allusions.

answer.text: To penalize widely dispersed word co-occurrences and reward tight syntactic clustering characteristic of audible literary echoes.

feedback.text: Correct. Words occurring in the same line or phrase are far more likely to represent deliberate allusions than words scattered across distant paragraphs.

answer.text: To calculate the physical geographical distance between the libraries where the manuscripts are stored.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Distance refers strictly to token distance within the text stream, not physical geography.

answer.text: To force the algorithm to search only documents that were published in the same calendar year.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The distance divisor measures word separation within poetic lines, not publication dates.

answer.text: To ensure that longer books always receive higher intertextual scores than short poems.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Longer books with widely dispersed words are penalized by the distance divisor.

name.text: 08 Question: Tuning Precision and Recall in Tesserae

questiontext.text: What is the practical consequence of setting a very low score threshold (e.g., Score $\ge 3.0$) in Tesserae?

generalfeedback.text: Editors must deliberately calibrate score thresholds to balance high recall (capturing subtle echoes) against high precision (filtering out coincidental noise).

answer.text: It achieves high recall by capturing subtle allusions, but yields very low precision by flooding the editor with thousands of coincidental matches.

feedback.text: Correct. A low threshold casts a wide net that catches subtle allusions alongside immense formulaic and grammatical noise.

answer.text: The algorithm crashes because modern computers cannot process scores lower than 5.0.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The software handles low scores easily; the burden falls on the human editor who must filter the noisy results.

answer.text: It filters out all verbatim quotations and returns only non-existent fabricated allusions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Verbatim quotations receive high scores and remain in the results; low thresholds add low-scoring noise.

answer.text: It automatically locks the digital edition repository to prevent further editing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Threshold tuning is an analytical search parameter, not a repository permission setting.

name.text: 09 Question: What Deterministic Algorithms Catch

questiontext.text: Which category of intertextual connection do deterministic algorithms discover with exceptional efficacy?

generalfeedback.text: Deterministic tools excel at surfacing verbatim loans, formulaic repetitions, and obscure borrowings from sub-canonical literature that human readers miss.

answer.text: Verbatim quotations, formulaic epic phrases, rare compound words, and unanthologized borrowings from sub-canonical authors.

feedback.text: Correct. Lexical matching algorithms excel at finding shared words across massive corpora, especially in neglected or obscure texts that human readers overlook.

answer.text: Ironic parodies that use completely different vocabulary to mock an earlier poem.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Purely lexical algorithms are blind to parodies and allusions that share no surface vocabulary.

answer.text: Translations between ancient Greek poetry and classical Latin verse.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Monolingual lexical algorithms cannot detect cross-linguistic translations without bilingual semantic mapping.

answer.text: Metaphorical themes that share conceptual meaning without sharing any common lemmas.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Deterministic tools require shared lexical tokens to calculate similarity scores.

name.text: 10 Question: What Deterministic Algorithms Miss

questiontext.text: Why is Tesserae completely blind to Ovid's metapoetic parody of Vergil in Amores 1.1 or Catullus's translation of Sappho?

generalfeedback.text: Deterministic algorithms are blind to synonymic substitutions, structural parodies, cross-linguistic translations, and thematic resonances that lack shared lemmas.

answer.text: Deterministic algorithms rely strictly on shared lexical lemmas, making them blind to synonymic substitutions, structural parodies, and cross-linguistic translations.

feedback.text: Correct. Because Tesserae matches identical lemmas, it cannot detect literary borrowing where the author translates from another language or alters the vocabulary.

answer.text: Ovid and Catullus wrote in an encrypted dialect that modern computers cannot decode.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Ovid and Catullus wrote in classical Latin; the limitation lies in the algorithm's reliance on lexical overlap rather than semantic comprehension.

answer.text: The Tesserae database excludes all love poetry and elegiac verse by design.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Tesserae indexes all major classical genres; the blind spot is structural and conceptual, not corpus exclusion.

answer.text: Tesserae only operates on texts composed after the invention of the printing press.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Tesserae was specifically built for ancient Greek and Latin classical literature.

name.text: 11 Question: Auditing Tesserae Output Against Tuesday's Manual Ground Truth

questiontext.text: What is the primary scholarly role of deterministic text-reuse algorithms in a digital commentary workflow?

generalfeedback.text: Auditing algorithmic output against manual ground truth reveals that algorithms function as powerful heuristic discovery engines requiring human critical vetting.

answer.text: They function as powerful heuristic discovery engines whose candidate leads must be critically vetted by a human-in-the-loop.

feedback.text: Correct. Algorithms rapidly surface prospective textual parallels across vast corpora, but human judgment is required to distinguish authentic allusions from coincidental noise.

answer.text: They serve as autonomous authoring agents that replace the need for peer review.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Computational algorithms generate unverified candidate matches that require human verification.

answer.text: They prove conclusively that later authors committed intentional copyright theft.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Ancient literary culture valued mimesis and imitation; algorithmic matches provide textual evidence, not legal judgments.

answer.text: They automatically delete any manual notes that were not predicted by the algorithm.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The human ground-truth notes evaluate the algorithm, not the reverse.

name.text: 12 Question: Moving from Document-Internal Markup to Linked Open Annotations

questiontext.text: What primary limitation of document-internal TEI XML motivated the development of the W3C Web Annotation Data Model?

generalfeedback.text: The W3C Web Annotation Data Model transforms commentary from document-internal XML into independent, web-native Linked Open Data graphs.

answer.text: Internal XML notes are trapped in single-document silos, cannot easily participate in distributed web networks, and require write access to the host file.

feedback.text: Correct. The W3C standard externalizes commentary into web-native Linked Open Data (JSON-LD), allowing third parties to annotate documents across the web independently.

answer.text: TEI XML files cannot be stored on modern computer hard drives without data corruption.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI XML is extremely stable; the issue is web-native interoperability across distributed servers.

answer.text: Modern web browsers refuse to render HTML pages that contain XML elements.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Browsers render HTML converted from XML daily; W3C annotations provide open graph interoperability.

answer.text: The TEI Consortium officially banned all commentary notes in version 5 of its guidelines.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI P5 fully supports commentary; W3C WADM provides a complementary web-native linked data standard.

name.text: 13 Question: The W3C Web Annotation Data Model

questiontext.text: What three core components comprise the tripartite graph structure of a W3C Web Annotation?

generalfeedback.text: The W3C Web Annotation model structures commentary into three decoupled components: the Annotation metadata node, the interpretive Body, and the targeted Text.

answer.text: The Annotation metadata node, the interpretive Body (payload), and the targeted Text/Resource.

feedback.text: Correct. The W3C model cleanly separates the Annotation event (provenance, motivation) from what is being attached (Body) and what is being annotated (Target).

answer.text: The Database table, the SQL query, and the Output CSV spreadsheet.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These describe relational database operations, not the W3C Web Annotation graph model.

answer.text: The Input prompt, the Neural weight matrix, and the Generated token stream.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These describe machine learning architectures, not the WADM graph specification.

answer.text: The Author name, the Book price, and the ISBN barcode number.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These are bibliographic trade metadata fields, not the components of a web annotation.

name.text: 14 Question: JSON-LD Serialization of Web Annotations

questiontext.text: Why is JSON-LD used as the native serialization format for W3C Web Annotations?

generalfeedback.text: JSON-LD serializes W3C Web Annotations into standard web-native objects that combine developer simplicity with semantic RDF graph power.

answer.text: It combines developer-friendly JSON syntax with formal semantic RDF graph capabilities defined by @context.

feedback.text: Correct. JSON-LD allows web developers to manipulate annotations as standard JSON objects while enabling triplestores to parse them as Linked Open Data RDF graphs.

answer.text: It encrypts commentary notes so that only paid subscribers can read them.

feedback.text: Incorrect. JSON-LD is an open, human-readable data serialization format, not an encryption protocol.

answer.text: It converts all ancient languages into binary machine code for microprocessor execution.

feedback.text: Incorrect. JSON-LD preserves text strings and character encodings in standard UTF-8.

answer.text: It automatically submits all student notes to Google Search for indexing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. JSON-LD structures data according to W3C ontologies; search indexing is a separate process.

name.text: 15 Question: The Taxonomy of Scholarly Motivations in W3C WADM

questiontext.text: How does declaring a formal W3C motivation (such as commenting or identifying) benefit an edition?

generalfeedback.text: The W3C motivation taxonomy (commenting, identifying, linking, classifying) formally declares scholarly intent, enabling multi-layered interface filtering.

answer.text: It formally declares the scholarly intent of the note, enabling downstream digital interfaces to filter, style, and query annotation layers dynamically.

feedback.text: Correct. Declaring motivations allows readers to toggle specific layers—such as displaying only 'identifying' gazetteer links on a map while hiding apparatus notes.

answer.text: It determines how many points a student receives on their digital humanities homework assignment.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Motivation is an ontological classification of scholarly intent in the WADM standard, not a grading rubric.

answer.text: It forces the web browser to play an audio chime whenever an annotation is clicked.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Motivations provide semantic metadata for application logic, not hard-coded audio effects.

answer.text: It prevents other scholars from disagreeing with the editor's interpretation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Motivations structure scholarly dialogue and data filtering; they do not enforce interpretive uniformity.

name.text: 16 Question: Anchoring Challenges on the Dynamic Web

questiontext.text: Why do pure character offsets and XPath DOM selectors fail when anchoring annotations across dynamic web editions?

generalfeedback.text: Dynamic web environments cause brittle character offsets and DOM paths to break; resilient web commentary requires robust multi-layered selectors.

answer.text: Website CMS redesigns, template updates, and upstream typo corrections alter DOM tree paths and character indices, causing annotations to break or orphan.

feedback.text: Correct. Dynamic web pages shift structure frequently; relying purely on DOM paths or byte offsets results in broken or misaligned annotation anchors.

answer.text: Web servers automatically delete any annotation that is older than 24 hours.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Annotations persist; the failure is anchor misalignment caused by document modifications.

answer.text: HTML5 prohibits links from pointing to text inside paragraph elements.

feedback.text: Incorrect. HTML5 fully supports links and text selection; the challenge is maintaining anchor stability across revisions.

answer.text: Character offsets require proprietary software licenses that university libraries cannot afford.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Character offsets are simple integers; their limitation is fragility under text revisions.

name.text: 17 Question: Resilient Selectors: TextQuoteSelector and Context Windows

questiontext.text: How does the W3C TextQuoteSelector guarantee resilient anchor recovery across document revisions?

generalfeedback.text: The TextQuoteSelector ensures anchor survival across website redesigns by storing exact target strings bounded by prefix and suffix context windows.

answer.text: It records the exact target string flanked by prefix and suffix context windows, enabling unique triangulation and fuzzy healing.

feedback.text: Correct. Storing the exact string along with surrounding prefix and suffix text allows annotation clients to relocate the target even if HTML structure changes or minor typos are fixed.

answer.text: It permanently locks the target web page so that no future edits can ever be made to the text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TextQuoteSelector accommodates ongoing document revisions rather than locking files.

answer.text: It replaces the entire source text with a static screenshot image of the original webpage.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TextQuoteSelector operates on plain text strings and Unicode code points, not static image captures.

answer.text: It requires the author of the webpage to re-type the annotation by hand after every update.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Client software uses the context window to re-anchor the annotation automatically.

name.text: 18 Question: Positional Selectors: TextPositionSelector and Fragment Selectors

questiontext.text: What is the distinct advantage of using a FragmentSelector conforming to W3C Media Fragments?

generalfeedback.text: Positional and fragment selectors provide high-speed character indexing and multi-modal spatial anchoring to IIIF manuscript images.

answer.text: It allows commentary notes to anchor directly to spatial bounding boxes on IIIF manuscript images or temporal intervals in audio/video recordings.

feedback.text: Correct. Fragment selectors (e.g., xywh=160,240,800,600 or t=120,145) enable multi-modal annotations anchored to high-resolution manuscript scans and media.

answer.text: It automatically repairs physically torn parchment leaves in museum collections.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Fragment selectors provide digital spatial coordinates, not physical conservation.

answer.text: It compresses high-resolution images into tiny low-quality thumbnails to save network bandwidth.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Fragment selectors target specific sub-regions of full-resolution IIIF images via standard URI syntax.

answer.text: It restricts the user to reading only one sentence of the text at a time.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Fragment selectors specify target coordinates for annotations without restricting text reading.

name.text: 19 Question: Composing Selector Chains for Maximum Durability

questiontext.text: How does a multi-tiered selector cascade (e.g. XPath $\rightarrow$ Position $\rightarrow$ Quote $\rightarrow$ Fuzzy) operate in practice?

generalfeedback.text: Selector chains combine fast DOM/positional lookups with resilient text-quote context matching to provide robust, fail-safe web anchoring.

answer.text: It attempts fast DOM and positional indexing first, gracefully falling back to resilient text-quote context matching if the document structure was modified.

feedback.text: Correct. Selector chains combine high-speed rendering with robust fallback resilience, ensuring annotations load instantly when possible and survive document edits.

answer.text: It rejects any annotation that does not match all four selectors simultaneously with 100% byte equality.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The cascade is a fallback sequence where subsequent selectors resolve the target if earlier ones fail.

answer.text: It deletes the source document if any single selector in the chain fails to resolve.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Selector chains provide graceful degradation to protect document and annotation integrity.

answer.text: It randomly selects one selector from the list using a pseudo-random number generator.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Selector cascades follow a deterministic, prioritized hierarchy of resolution attempts.

name.text: 20 Question: Collaborative Annotation with Recogito 2

questiontext.text: How does Recogito 2 bridge the gap between humanistic scholars and semantic web standards?

generalfeedback.text: Recogito 2 demonstrates how intuitive graphical interfaces can generate standards-compliant W3C Web Annotations aligned with global gazetteers.

answer.text: It provides an intuitive web interface for highlighting texts and IIIF images, automatically generating W3C JSON-LD annotations aligned with global gazetteers.

feedback.text: Correct. Recogito removes the barrier of manual XML/RDF coding by allowing scholars to tag entities visually while exporting standards-compliant Linked Open Data.

answer.text: It automatically translates ancient Greek manuscripts into modern Danish without human review.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Recogito is an annotation platform for human scholars to align entities and realia, not a machine translation bot.

answer.text: It restricts all digital editing exclusively to printed books published before 1900.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Recogito ingests modern digital texts, TEI XML, and IIIF manuscript images.

answer.text: It replaces all human editors with unsupervised neural network agents.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Recogito was built specifically to empower human domain experts to create semantic annotations easily.

name.text: 21 Question: Semantic Annotation with Net7 Pundit

questiontext.text: What advanced capability distinguishes Net7 Pundit from basic web bookmarking tools?

generalfeedback.text: Net7 Pundit formalizes commentary into machine-readable RDF triples, bridging textual notes with global semantic knowledge graphs.

answer.text: It enables scholars to author formal semantic RDF triples (Subject-Predicate-Object) anchored to web text using controlled ontologies like CiTO.

feedback.text: Correct. Pundit allows researchers to create structured, machine-readable scholarly assertions that connect text spans to linked data entities via formal ontological predicates.

answer.text: It automatically posts web links to social media feeds every time a user highlights text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Pundit creates structured RDF linked data for digital libraries, not social media posts.

answer.text: It converts entire websites into static PDF files that cannot be edited or annotated.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Pundit operates directly on live web documents, creating dynamic semantic knowledge graphs.

answer.text: It deletes any web page that contains grammatical errors or spelling mistakes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Pundit is an annotation tool for scholarly research, not a destructive web filter.

name.text: 22 Question: Open Web Annotation in Practice: Hypothes.is

questiontext.text: Why is Hypothes.is widely adopted for collaborative commentary in digital humanities teaching and research?

generalfeedback.text: Hypothes.is provides an open, collaborative web annotation layer that implements W3C standards and connects directly to digital edition workflows via REST APIs.

answer.text: It injects a standards-compliant W3C annotation layer over any web edition or PDF, enabling collaborative group reviews and REST API data extraction.

feedback.text: Correct. Hypothes.is works over any public web document without server access, supports private/public groups, and provides a REST API to export W3C JSON-LD.

answer.text: It replaces student grading with an automated algorithmic cryptocurrency reward system.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hypothes.is is an open-source educational and scholarly annotation platform.

answer.text: It prevents students from reading commentary written by previous generations of scholars.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hypothes.is supports shared public and group annotation layers to foster collaborative dialogue.

answer.text: It requires all users to write their commentary notes exclusively in raw binary machine code.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hypothes.is provides an intuitive rich-text and Markdown interface for authoring notes.

name.text: 23 Question: Case Study: DanteSources and Knowledge Graphs

questiontext.text: How did the DanteSources project transform traditional literary commentary on Dante's works into a queryable knowledge graph?

generalfeedback.text: DanteSources illustrates how integrating formal ontologies (FRBRoo, DoCO, CiTO) transforms traditional narrative commentary into queryable knowledge graphs.

answer.text: By developing an integrated ontology combining FRBRoo, DoCO, and CiTO to model Dante's texts, structural divisions, and citation relationships as RDF triples.

feedback.text: Correct. DanteSources structured narrative commentary into semantic triples linking cantos and lines to primary sources (e.g. Aristotle, Virgil) via typed citation relationships.

answer.text: By deleting all references to classical pagan authors and replacing them with modern commentary.

feedback.text: Incorrect. DanteSources meticulously mapped Dante's classical and medieval sources rather than deleting them.

answer.text: By converting the Divine Comedy into an animated 3D video game.

feedback.text: Incorrect. DanteSources is a digital scholarly library and semantic knowledge graph for research.

answer.text: By proving that Dante authored all of his poems using automated computational algorithms.

feedback.text: Incorrect. DanteSources analyzes historical reception and primary source citations in Dante's authentic works.

name.text: 24 Question: SPARQL Querying of Intertextual Networks

questiontext.text: What type of research analysis does a SPARQL endpoint enable across linked commentary networks?

generalfeedback.text: SPARQL queries allow researchers to execute relational, distant-reading analyses across linked intertextual commentary networks.

answer.text: Complex relational and distant-reading queries across distributed corpora, such as finding all explicit citations of a specific author across structural cantos.

feedback.text: Correct. SPARQL enables cross-corpus semantic queries that extract patterns of citation, authorial influence, and thematic development without linear manual searching.

answer.text: Editing the raw binary firmware of the computer's motherboard.

feedback.text: Incorrect. SPARQL is a semantic query language for RDF graphs, not hardware firmware software.

answer.text: Automatically rewriting ancient poetry to match modern 21st-century political views.

feedback.text: Incorrect. SPARQL retrieves and queries existing structured data; it does not rewrite primary sources.

answer.text: Calculating the financial profitability of commercial print publishers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. SPARQL queries scholarly and bibliographic knowledge graphs, not commercial corporate financials.

name.text: 25 Question: Hands-On Exercise: Running Tesserae on the Test Corpus

questiontext.text: When running a deterministic Tesserae search, why is it essential to configure a stoplist and maximum distance cutoff?

generalfeedback.text: Running Tesserae with configured stoplists and distance cutoffs generates a scored, ranked list of candidate intertextual matches.

answer.text: To filter out ubiquitous function words and eliminate diffuse word co-occurrences that generate massive non-allusive noise.

feedback.text: Correct. Configuring stoplists and distance windows restricts candidate generation to meaningful, compact lexical clusters, keeping output manageable.

answer.text: To force the algorithm to run only on odd-numbered days of the week.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Parameter configuration controls linguistic filtering and spatial windows, not calendar schedules.

answer.text: To delete all punctuation from the primary manuscript permanently.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Parameters govern search execution without altering master repository files.

answer.text: To prevent third-party scholars from reproducing the search results.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Explicit parameter documentation ensures reproducibility across research teams.

name.text: 26 Question: Hands-On Exercise: Scoring and Filtering Deterministic Matches

questiontext.text: How do editors quantitatively benchmark the performance of a deterministic search against manual ground truth?

generalfeedback.text: Evaluating candidate matches against manual ground truth produces quantitative precision and recall metrics that benchmark algorithmic efficiency.

answer.text: By calculating precision (true positives divided by total returned matches) and recall (true positives divided by total known ground-truth allusions).

feedback.text: Correct. Precision measures how many returned matches are genuine, while recall measures how many authentic historical allusions the algorithm successfully retrieved.

answer.text: By measuring the physical temperature of the computer's central processing unit during the search.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Performance benchmarking in information retrieval evaluates precision and recall, not CPU temperature.

answer.text: By counting the total number of spelling mistakes made by the student in their lab notebook.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Algorithmic benchmarking evaluates true positives, false positives, and false negatives.

answer.text: By multiplying the number of returned matches by the cost of university tuition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Quantitative metrics evaluate algorithmic accuracy against empirical human data.

name.text: 27 Question: Hands-On Exercise: Converting TEI Annotations to W3C JSON-LD

questiontext.text: What key transformation occurs when converting a TEI stand-off <note> into a W3C Web Annotation JSON-LD object?

generalfeedback.text: Converting TEI stand-off notes into W3C JSON-LD creates multi-body, multi-selector web annotations ready for distributed semantic consumption.

answer.text: The note becomes an independent web resource with a unique URI, a typed motivation, a multi-part body, and a resilient selector.

feedback.text: Correct. Converting to W3C JSON-LD externalizes the note into a web-native graph object equipped with LOD URIs and context-window selectors.

answer.text: The note is stripped of all historical metadata and converted into an unformatted plain text email.

feedback.text: Incorrect. JSON-LD preserves and expands semantic metadata within a formal RDF context.

answer.text: The XML elements are translated into mathematical calculus equations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. JSON-LD is a data serialization format representing web annotation graphs.

answer.text: The note is automatically deleted from the local Git repository.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Local TEI XML is preserved for archival storage while JSON-LD is generated for web dissemination.

name.text: 28 Question: Hands-On Exercise: Deploying Annotations via Hypothes.is / Web Client

questiontext.text: What does programmatic verification via the Hypothes.is REST API demonstrate about an edition's commentary?
